## tool-budget

**MCS001** · suggestion · surface · stable

Limit the number of tools a server exposes in its default configuration.

Every tool definition is sent to the model on every turn. Past roughly 15 tools, tool-selection accuracy drops and context cost grows. Servers that need more capability should split into focused servers or expose toolsets that clients enable on demand. The rule counts the tools the snapshot saw, so snapshot the default configuration to measure what users get out of the box.

Source: Rodrigues & Vas, ICSME 2026: tool budget of about 10-15 tools per server

Options (defaults shown):

```json
{
  "tool-budget": [
    "warn",
    {
      "max": 15
    }
  ]
}
```

Messages:

- Server exposes `<count>` tools, over the budget of `<max>`. Split it into focused servers or ship smaller default toolsets.

## missing-description

**MCS101** · problem · descriptions · stable

Every tool needs a description.

The description is the only thing the model reads to decide whether to call a tool. A tool without one is chosen by name alone, which leads to wrong or missed calls.

Source: Rodrigues & Vas, ICSME 2026: Missing/Vague Descriptions anti-pattern

Messages:

- Tool '`<tool>`' has no description.

## vague-description

**MCS102** · suggestion · descriptions · stable

Tool descriptions should say more than the tool name.

A description that only restates the name (list_gateways: "List Gateways") or is a couple of words long gives the model nothing to choose with: no scope, no inputs, no when-to-use. The rule flags descriptions under `minWords` words and descriptions whose words, ignoring filler, all come from the tool name.

Source: Rodrigues & Vas, ICSME 2026: Missing/Vague Descriptions anti-pattern

Options (defaults shown):

```json
{
  "vague-description": [
    "warn",
    {
      "minWords": 4
    }
  ]
}
```

Messages:

- Tool '`<tool>`' has a `<count>`-word description. Say what it returns and when to use it.
- Tool '`<tool>`' description only restates its name. Say what it returns and when to use it.

## missing-parameter-description

**MCS103** · suggestion · descriptions · stable

Tool input properties should have descriptions.

Models fill arguments from the property name and description. Undescribed parameters lead to guessed formats (ids vs names, relative vs absolute paths). Enum-valued properties can be skipped with `ignoreEnums`, since the allowed values already document them.

Source: Rodrigues & Vas, ICSME 2026: Missing/Vague Descriptions anti-pattern

Options (defaults shown):

```json
{
  "missing-parameter-description": [
    "warn",
    {
      "ignore": [],
      "ignoreEnums": false
    }
  ]
}
```

Messages:

- Parameter '`<param>`' of tool '`<tool>`' has no description.

## god-tool-dispatch

**MCS201** · suggestion · god-tool · stable

Avoid tools that dispatch many operations through one selector argument.

A tool such as `pull_request_read(method: get | get_diff | get_files | ...)` hides several operations behind one name and one description. The model must pick the tool and then the right method, the description has to cover every operation, and annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint) can only describe the riskiest one. The rule flags a selector-named property (method, action, operation, command, ...) or a discriminated union with at least `minOperations` allowed values. Vendors often consolidate on purpose to stay within a tool budget; if so, group operations by risk class (all reads in one tool, writes in another) rather than mixing them.

Source: Rodrigues & Vas, ICSME 2026: God Tool anti-pattern

Options (defaults shown):

```json
{
  "god-tool-dispatch": [
    "warn",
    {
      "minOperations": 4,
      "selectorNames": [
        "method",
        "action",
        "operation",
        "op",
        "command",
        "cmd",
        "mode",
        "subcommand",
        "verb",
        "intent",
        "function"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Messages:

- Tool '`<tool>`' dispatches `<count>` operations through '`<selector>`' (`<operations>`). Split it into one tool per operation, or at least per risk class.
- Tool '`<tool>`' dispatches `<count>` operations through '`<selector>`', mixing reads and writes (`<operations>`). Split it at least by risk class.

## god-tool-passthrough

**MCS202** · suggestion · god-tool · preview

Flag tools that pass free-form commands, code, or HTTP requests through to an underlying system.

A passthrough tool (run any CLI command, execute any code, send any HTTP request) is the limit case of a God Tool: its operation set is unbounded, so neither its description nor its annotations can describe what a call does, and approval prompts show an opaque string. The rule flags a free-form string parameter named like code or a command (command, code, script, sql, ...) on a tool whose name or description talks about executing, and generic HTTP tools that take a method and a path. This is a preview rule: passthrough tools are sometimes the product, so treat findings as design review items.

Source: mcpsmell pilot (Nov 2026): passthrough variant of the God Tool, seen in AWS call_aws, kubectl_generic, Supabase postgrestRequest

Messages:

- Tool '`<tool>`' passes free-form '`<param>`' through for execution. Prefer typed operations, or scope and document what it may run.
- Tool '`<tool>`' is a generic HTTP passthrough ('`<method>`' + '`<url>`'). Prefer typed operations per endpoint.

## coarse-annotations

**MCS301** · problem · annotations · stable

A tool that mixes read and write operations cannot carry accurate safety annotations.

Clients use readOnlyHint and destructiveHint to decide when to ask the user for approval. Annotations apply to the whole tool, so a dispatch tool that both lists and deletes must either claim to be read-only (unsafe: writes skip approval) or destructive (noisy: every read asks for approval). The rule reports a mixed dispatch tool as a problem when it claims readOnlyHint: true, and as a coarse annotation otherwise.

Source: MCP spec tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint); mcpsmell pilot finding on God Tools

Options (defaults shown):

```json
{
  "coarse-annotations": [
    "warn",
    {
      "minOperations": 2
    }
  ]
}
```

Messages:

- Tool '`<tool>`' is annotated readOnlyHint: true but its '`<selector>`' includes writes (`<writes>`). Clients may skip approval for them.
- Tool '`<tool>`' mixes read (`<reads>`) and write (`<writes>`) operations, so one set of annotations cannot describe it. Split reads from writes.

## version-suffixed-name

**MCS401** · suggestion · naming · stable

Do not version tools through their names (search_v2, get_items_new).

Models cannot tell which of search and search_v2 to use, and agents tend to call both. Versions belong in the server version reported in initialize; replace tools in place and remove the old one, or keep distinct names that say what differs.

Source: Srinivasan, arXiv 2603.13417: version-suffixed tool names

Messages:

- Tool '`<tool>`' carries a version or age suffix in its name.

## hidden-instructions

**MCS501** · problem · security · preview

Flag tool and parameter descriptions that carry instructions aimed at the model rather than documentation.

Descriptions are injected into the model's context verbatim. Poisoned descriptions hide instructions in invisible Unicode, pseudo tags like <IMPORTANT>, requests to ignore previous instructions, requests to keep something from the user, or references to credential files. These are regular-expression signals: they have false positives (a security tool may mention .env legitimately) and miss paraphrases, so this is a preview rule and findings need review.

Source: Shaikh & Montaruli, arXiv 2611.03555 (tool poisoning); Invariant Labs mcp-scan tool-poisoning checks

Messages:

- `<where>` contains invisible Unicode characters.
- `<where>` contains a pseudo-tag (`<match>`) addressed to the model.
- `<where>` asks the model to ignore other instructions.
- `<where>` asks the model to hide something from the user.
- `<where>` references a credential or config file (`<match>`).
